title: Schools of Psychology
summary: The major schools of psychology - Structuralism, Functionalism, Behaviourism, Psychoanalysis, Gestalt, Humanistic, Cognitive and Existential - with founders, core subject, method, legacy and criticisms, plus a three-way comparison and examination practice.

notes.t: The major schools of psychology emerged in roughly this order: Structuralism (1896), Functionalism (1896), Psychoanalysis (1900), Gestalt Psychology (1912), Behaviourism (1913), Humanistic Psychology (1954) and Cognitive Psychology (1956).

notes.c: Major schools of psychology - founders, core subject and method

notes.t: Structuralism was one of the earliest systematic schools of modern psychology. It attempted to understand the structure of conscious experience by analysing it into its fundamental components. Titchener, a student of Wilhelm Wundt, brought Wundt's ideas to Cornell University in the United States.
The school that studies the structure of conscious experience by analysing it into basic elements, using introspection as its primary method.

Assumptions: consciousness can be broken down into basic elements; the structure of the mind is the proper subject of psychology. Method: introspection — trained observers report their own sensations, images and feelings under controlled conditions, avoiding 'stimulus-error' (naming the object instead of reporting the sensation).

r: Mental image of a familiar place

notes.t: Applications: structuralism established psychology as an experimental, laboratory-based discipline. Criticisms: introspection is subjective and not verifiable by others; it cannot study children, animals or abnormal behaviour; the subject matter is too narrow.

Behaviourism emphasises the study of observable behaviours rather than internal mental states. Watson's 1913 manifesto, 'Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It', argued that psychology should study only observable behaviour because consciousness is not observable and hence not scientific.
The school that studies only observable behaviour, holding that the environment shapes behaviour through conditioning (stimulus–response, S→R).

Key ideas: stimulus–response (S→R); classical conditioning (Pavlov, extended by Watson); the Little Albert experiment (1920); operant conditioning, later expanded by B.F. Skinner, which explains how behaviours are strengthened or weakened through reinforcement and punishment.

Applications: behaviour therapy, behaviour modification, education and advertising. Criticisms: ignores internal mental processes; ethical concerns (Little Albert); deterministic view of human behaviour.

Gestalt is a German word meaning 'an organized whole' or 'configuration.' Gestalt psychology emerged in Germany as a response to structuralism's elementism. Gestalt psychologists argued that perception is more than just the sum of its parts — when we observe the world, our perceptual experience is shaped by how different elements interact to form a unified whole.
Key ideas: perceptual grouping (proximity, similarity, closure, continuity); insight learning (Köhler's chimpanzee Sultan); the phi phenomenon.

notes.c: Side-by-side comparison of the eight schools

notes.t: Core distinction: Structuralism asks what the mind is made of; Functionalism asks what the mind does; Behaviourism restricts psychology to observable behaviour. This distinction recurs in matching and assertion–reasoning questions.

mnemonics.title: School founders in chronological order
mnemonics.text: Wundt, Titchener, James, Watson, Freud, Gestalt (WTJWFG). Matches order of emergence: Wundt (1879 laboratory), Titchener (Structuralism), James (Functionalism), Watson (Behaviourism, 1913), Freud (Psychoanalysis), Gestalt (1912). Say it as a chant — 'Witch-waffle' — and attach each founder to his school and date as you recite.
